summary: Surveys current practices large ISPs use to secure layer 2 and layer 3 infrastructure devices, based on information from people responsible for those networks. It is informational and does not set new rules.

eli5.summary: This is a report of how big internet providers lock down their own network equipment, collected by asking the people who do it. It describes what is done, not what must be done.

subtitle: How large ISPs protect their network infrastructure from attacks

tldr.problem: Large ISPs face constant threats to their network infrastructure from reconnaissance, spoofing, and denial-of-service attacks. Without security practices, attackers could compromise routers and disrupt service.
tldr.mechanism: ISPs deploy multi-layered defenses: physical access controls and console authentication for devices, SSH and AAA authentication for remote management, MD5-based routing security, filtering to block spoofed traffic, comprehensive logging, and specialized DoS mitigation techniques.
tldr.outcome: This RFC documents how the industry currently secures layer 2 and layer 3 infrastructure in practice. It is informational and does not mandate new standards, but captures existing best practices that have proven effective.

today: RFC 4778 is an Informational document that remains relevant. It documents practices from large ISPs circa 2007. The practices described are still widely used, though some details have evolved. Newer threats and technologies (IPv6, cloud infrastructure, DDoS services) have prompted additional security measures, but the core approaches of authentication, encryption, filtering, and logging documented here remain foundational to ISP security.

sections.title: Introduction and Threat Model
sections.content:
The RFC surveys current security practices in large Internet Service Provider networks to secure infrastructure devices. The threats come from several directions: reconnaissance (gathering information about network topology), man-in-the-middle attacks (intercepting and modifying traffic), protocol exploitation (using protocol design flaws), and message insertion (injecting forged packets). Attacks can be active (writing to the network) or passive (eavesdropping), on-path (control intermediate devices) or off-path (no direct network access), and from insiders or outsiders.

The impact of successful attacks can be disclosure (unauthorized access to data), deception (receiving false information), disruption (denial of service), or usurpation (unauthorized control of devices and network functions).
sections.eli5: Bad guys try different tricks: they might watch the network to learn its layout, pretend to be a router to redirect traffic, use tricks the protocol designers did not plan for, or flood the network with fake messages. These attacks can steal information, fool the network, break service, or take control of equipment.

sections.title: Securing Device Management
sections.content:
Device management is how network operators configure and monitor routers and switches. The survey found that large ISPs use both out-of-band (OOB) management (a separate network for control traffic) and in-band management (control traffic mixed with customer data). All management uses strong authentication via AAA servers (RADIUS or TACACS+), with individual user accounts and privilege levels. SSH is the standard protocol for remote terminal access because it provides encryption and data integrity. SNMP is used for monitoring only, with read-only access and shared secret rotation every 30 to 90 days. HTTP management is explicitly disabled on all large ISPs surveyed.

Access control is strict: only specific IP addresses can initiate management connections to infrastructure devices. Every access attempt is logged, and abnormal activity triggers automated alerts. Some legacy equipment still requires Telnet, but only from hardened "jumphost" servers that limit the exposure.
sections.eli5: When engineers want to fix a router, they log in with a unique username and password. The login uses encryption so a snooper cannot steal the password. The system records who logged in and what they did. Only trusted computers can connect to the routers, and the system alerts operators immediately if someone suspicious tries.

sections.title: Protecting Routing Control Plane
sections.content:
The routing control plane exchanges route information between routers. Attacks here can redirect traffic to unintended destinations. ISPs use several defenses: MD5 authentication on routing protocol exchanges to verify the sender and ensure data has not been modified. The Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM) feature adds a check on the TTL field to prevent off-path routers from spoofing routing updates. Route filters and prefix limits prevent routers from accepting invalid or misconfigured announcements. In BGP, ISPs implement strict prefix filtering, AS-PATH filtering, and route dampening. Some ISPs require routes to be registered in the Internet Routing Registry before accepting them from peers.

Despite these tools, MD5 authentication is not consistently deployed due to operational concerns about CPU impact and lack of graceful re-keying options. GTSM support varies across vendor equipment.
sections.eli5: Before a router accepts a route update from another router, it checks a signature to make sure the message really came from that router and has not been changed. It also checks if the sender is close enough (via TTL), and it rejects route updates that look obviously wrong, like announcing routes it should not have.

sections.title: Filtering and DoS Mitigation
sections.content:
Customer data passing through the network is filtered to block malicious traffic. ISPs implement BCP38 and BCP84 ingress filtering to drop packets with obviously spoofed source addresses. Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding (uRPF) validates that packets arrive on the interface expected for their source address. Rate limiting and traffic shaping reduce the impact of flooding attacks. For ongoing DoS attacks, ISPs use black-hole triggered routing: when an attack is detected, a more specific route is announced that redirects attack traffic to a null route where it is dropped, using BGP to propagate the change quickly across the network. Sinkhole routing redirects attack traffic to a monitoring device for analysis.

Layer 4 filtering (blocking specific protocols or ports) is considered useful but deployed conservatively due to operational complexity. Netflow helps track traffic patterns to detect anomalies.
sections.eli5: Filters block packets that obviously cannot be real, like one claiming to come from inside the network but arriving from outside. If a big attack is happening, routers announce a rule that throws away those packets instantly. Network staff watch traffic patterns to spot unusual behavior and trace attacks back to their source.

sections.title: Configuration, Logging, and Verification
sections.content:
ISPs verify software and configuration integrity using CRC checks and MD5 signatures. Configuration files are stored on restricted servers and downloaded over authenticated channels (SCP when possible, TFTP with IP-based restrictions otherwise). Most ISP environments use tools like Rancid to poll configuration files hourly and detect changes. Passwords in configuration files are encrypted using vendor-specific encryption (some schemes are weak and subject to dictionary attacks).

Logging happens primarily on an exception basis (only violations are logged, not normal traffic) to avoid overwhelming logging servers with data. Syslog protocol sends logs from devices to central servers using the out-of-band network. NTP provides synchronized time across the network. All access to infrastructure devices is logged by AAA servers, and routing protocol changes, device boots, and access failures are recorded. Operators monitor these logs to detect intrusions or misconfigurations.

The RFC notes that syslog itself has no security; operators compensate by running syslog servers on protected out-of-band networks and restricting access to the logging infrastructure itself.
sections.eli5: When an engineer loads new software or a configuration onto a router, the router checks a signature to make sure it came from the vendor and was not tampered with. All changes are logged with timestamps. Logs go to protected servers that only authorized people can access. If anything suspicious happens—wrong password, unexpected change, attack blocked—the system records it and can alert the team immediately.

sections.title: Limitations and Open Challenges
sections.content:
The survey identified several limitations in current practice. IPsec is considered too operationally complex to deploy for routing control plane or data plane protection. SSH re-keying issues on some devices (key tied to hostname or MAC address) make rotation difficult. For networks with physical layer limitations, some ISPs fall back to Telnet from trusted hosts because deploying SSH everywhere would require re-keying infrastructure too frequently.

Layer 2 MAC address filtering and port security become unmanageable at scale. Rate limiting is controversial: some operators believe it is less effective than filtering and can paradoxically help attackers by requiring less traffic. The absence of performance-efficient filtering hardware limits deployment of BCP38 and BCP84 at very high-speed edges.

ISPs expressed desire for better syslog protocols with security, granular filtering facilities, and more flexible priority levels. OAM (Operations and Management) capabilities needed enhancement across the board. The document emphasizes that these practices reflect what operators are actually doing as of 2007, not what the ideal solution would be.
sections.eli5: Operators say they need better tools for encrypting syslog, more fine-grained control over what gets logged, and easier ways to configure encryption on old equipment. Some defensive techniques work better in theory than in practice because vendor products do not support them well, or they cause too much operational overhead.
